messages.subject: X'X matrix is singular.
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to do a QTL analysis in a cross of ~200 individuals with
~80 markers.  They relationships between the individuals are not as
simple as parent/child, however they were sampled from discrete
populations, A B and C.  Further, each population had a subset of
sampling, A1 A2 and A3 for example.  I am trying to use this
designation as a covariate in my QTL mapping, however the error is
always  X'X matrix is singular. No other errors appear, but this error
occurs 12-50 times. I read that this meant the model was
overdetermined, so I tried to reduce the model by using A B and C, but
I get the same result. Likewise, if I create a matrix with each a
separate column so that it is binary (instead of 1-9 since it must be
numeric, column A1 with 1's for A1's and 0's for everything else, etc
for each possible population) but the same thing happens. For
example:

cross<-as.numeric(pull.pheno(x2, "fam"))

A<-as.numeric(cross<4)

C<-as.numeric(cross>6)

B<-as.numeric(cross==4 | cross==6 | cross==5)

x2$pheno$A<-A

 x2$pheno$B<-B

x2$pheno$C<-C

 crossX<-cbind(A, B, C)

out.cov<-scanone(x2, pheno.col=2, addcovar=crossX)

There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50)
> warnings()
Warning messages:
1: In checkcovar(cross, pheno.col, addcovar, intcovar,
perm.strata,  ... :
  addcovar appears to be over-specified; consider dropping columns.

2: X'X matrix is singular.

I am clearly missing something fundamental, but if anyone as any
advice as to how to solve this problem I would appreciate it.

Thank you, Sarah

Thank you!!  Here is the code karl sent me to fix the problem, if that
helps anyone else.

out.cov[out.cov$chr=="1",] # problem is at the end of chr
1geno.table(x2, chr="1") # a bunch of monomorphic markers
# drop the monomorphic markersmn <- markernames(x, chr="1")mn2drop <-
mn[grep("1", mn)]x <- drop.markers(x, mn2drop)
# need to treat the family covariate as a set of 0/1 factorslev <-
levels(x$pheno$fam)X <- matrix(0, nrow=nind(x),
ncol=length(lev)-1)for(i in 2:length(lev))  X[x$pheno$fam==lev[i],i-1]
<- 1
out.cov2<-scanone(x, pheno.col=2, addcovar=X)

messages.subject: eQTL FDR through permutations
messages.body_plain:
I’m conducting an eQTL study in a RIL mapping population.  One
challenge is figuring out how to control for multiple testing with
thousands of transcripts.  One method I've seen in the literature is
an empirically derived FDR using permutations (Brem et al. 2002 in
Science, Smith & Kruglyak 2008 in PLoS Bio, Rockman et al. 2010 in
Science).  I would like to use this approach as a way to determine an
FDR threshold for my R/qtl scanone results.

The approach focuses on permuting the row labels of all of the
transcripts.  This will maintain the correlation structure among
expression traits while randomizing the individual genotype vectors
associated with each phenotype vector.  After each round of
permutation, I will extract the single highest LOD score per each
phenotype.  This will result in a vector with ~25000 LOD scores, one
LOD score for each transcript.  I plan to conduct many such rounds of
permutations and then use the results to calculate an FDR.  To do so I
will rank the LOD scores per each round and then calculate the mean
LOD per rank across all permutation rounds.  To calculate FDR = 0.05,
I will determine the LOD at which only 5% of the mean LOD scores are
ranked larger.  This FDR threshold will then be applied to the output
of interval mapping in the nonpermuted data as a threshold for QTL
significance across the entire data set.  Does this method seem
reasonable?

I’ve written some scripts to run this type of analysis but it is
computational intensive and involves several manipulations of data
outputs.  I’m wondering whether much of the existing scanone and
summary.scanoneperm will let me do a similar analysis.  For example,
if I run permutations on all my phenotypes together (phe.col= 1:25000)
are these completed by shuffling row labels (maintaining the
correlations structure)?  Also, the summary documentation mentions an
argument “controlAcrossCol” of “summary.scanoneperm.”  In that
documentation you write:

“If ‘controlAcrossCol=TRUE’, we use a trick to control the error rate
not just across the genome but also across the LOD score columns.
Namely, we convert each column of permutation results to ranks, and
then for each permutation replicate we find the maximum rank across
the columns.  We then find the appropriate quantile of the maximized
ranks, and then backtrack to the corresponding LOD score within each
of the columns.”

Is this implementing the “FDR” approach I describe above?  Please let
me know if I am misinterpreting this and thanks for your help.

David

messages.subject: Comparing summaries of imputations
messages.body_plain:
I am wondering if anyone can offer advice (or code) on summarizing
genotypes across imputations?

I would like to determine how much the results of an analysis might
change when run with different numbers of imputations, but it is much
too slow to wait for the full analyses.

Instead I thought I could look at the average (across imputations)
genotypes for each locus for say 32 imputations and again for say 512
imputations. If there is no difference, and this is repeatable, then
it seems safe to use the lower number of imputations for all future
analyses. Does this seem reasonable?

I know enough to save the imputations to file (separately by
chromosome), but am having trouble coming up with a functional bit of
code to summarize the file. Part of my problem is that actual marker
locations and imputed markers have different column name pattern, and
my grep-ing skills are not so great.

Any advice appreciated.

Thanks,

Chris

This doesn't use FDR but rather seeks to control the family-wise error rate (FWER).

messages.subject: Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map
messages.subject_clean: Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl Group:

I have a couple of questions for the R/qtl group, but first some background.

A Soybean Reference Genetic Map was constructed with JoinMap software using 5500 markers genotypes present in one or more of five different mapping populations of about 250 RILs.  This reference map was also used in the soybean DNA sequencing effort and the chromosomal bp location of the SNP and SSR markers are now known.

My research group has created 48 populations of about 200+ F2 plants each that were derived from matings of high x low seed protein parents - ALL F2.3 seed progenies were phenotyped in each population, but ONLY 44 F2 progenitors of the 22 highest and 22 lowest protein F2.3 progenies were selectively genotyped (SG) in each of the 48 F2 populations with about 500 parentally bimorphic markers of the reference map 5500 marker set.

Question 1:  Would it be reasonable to rely solely on the reference genetic map (i.e., marker orders and RIL-based inter-marker Kosambi distances) instead of each actual F2 map (i.e., marker orders and F2-based distances in each of the 48 SG pops) for conducting R/qtl pro & oil interval QTL analyses of the 48 F2 pops?  I ask this question because there was what I took to be an indirect mention of this issue in page 65 of the Broman and Sen book that contrasted a reference genetic map with actual genetic maps.

Note to Readers:  Except over small map distances (or over somewhat larger distances when there were missing F2 marker genotype data), I found the chromosomal marker orders in each of the 48 pops to be nearly identical with the chromosomal marker orders in the reference map.  This comparison was done AFTER conducting all of the Broman-recommended R/qtl marker genotype and F2 individual error checking methods mentioned in his R/qtl tutorials.  However, the recombination fraction values (and thus inter-marker map distances) in the actual genetic maps derived from the 44 genotypes in each SG'd 48 population are substantively larger (chromosomes are about 50-100 % longer in distance) than the reference map.  I am wondering if this chromosomal map length difference between the reference map and each of the 48 F2 genetic maps is of consequence relative to QTL analysis if the marker orders are the same, and if one can substitute reference map order AND reference map inter-marker map distances for the actual genetic maps in each of the 48 populations?

Question 2:  If one uses a csvr file in which the reference map marker order and it's Kosambi map distances are included with the F2 genotype data (44 of the 200+ F2 plants), how then does one handle the est.rf function for an R/qtl-based QTL analysis wherein some R/qtl commands may require the use of the est.rf function?  I ask this question given that I am inputting the selfed-RIL-based reference map Kosambi inter-marker distances (not the F2 derived distances), yet the execution of the est.rf function will use the F2 marker genotype data.  The observed (selfed) RIL recombination fraction R values are greater than observed F2 recombination values (i.e., per meiosis rf values), but can be related to each other by the standard Haldane and Waddington formula R = [(2r)/(1+2r)].  Does one incur a problem by putting RIL marker order and distances in a csvr file that contains F2 marker genotype data relative to doing a subsequent QTL analysis with the resultant genetic map?

Any replies to this post in the form of comments, opinions, insights, etc would be greatly appreciated.

- Jim

messages.subject: mqmaugment()
messages.body_plain:
So, I've been working with a O. sativa RIL population (~150
individuals) which has been genotyped via GBS (Genotyping by
sequencing) and have a set of about ~2K SNPs that I believe are the
best based on the confidence we have in their calls and have exhibited
the lowest amount of missing data. That being said, there is still a
good amount of missing data that we have taken great computational
care to impute. We only impute those data points that we believe can
reasonably be ascertained based on the extent of linkage
disequilibrium in that region of the genome.

So, now as I approach doing the mapping, everything I've read says
that the MQM implementation of R/QTL is the most sophisticated
function to be using, but I'm kind of concerned about having to use
mqmaugment() to fill in the remaining missing genotypes.

1) Can anyone shed some light on how the imputation works in this
function (is it simply a nearest neighbor kind of analysis?) and if I
am unnecessarily nervous about how it is "guessing" at the genotypes
of the missing data?

2) Am I worried unnecessarily? Is it likely that even if the
mqmaugment() inaccurately calls what little missing data is left after
I do my more sophisticated imputation that it will even make a
difference?

3) Would the CIM function be better in this case because it doesn't
mandate that their be no "NA" in the genotype data?

Any advice would be much appreciated. Thanks!
